analysis.one_liner: Restores the Glass-Steagall wall separating commercial banking from securities and investment banking.
analysis.headline: The Glass-Steagall restoration bill drew 84 cosponsors, including 4 Republicans, but never got a hearing or a vote in the House Financial Services Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rebuilt the Glass-Steagall separation, in place from 1933 until 1999, that barred commercial banks — the ones holding federally insured deposits — from being affiliated with investment banks, brokers, and securities dealers. It repealed the Gramm-Leach-Bliley provisions that allowed financial conglomerates like Citigroup to combine banking, trading, and underwriting under one roof, forced existing combinations to unwind within two years, and barred securities-firm executives from sitting on bank boards. It also locked in the Supreme Court's 1971 Investment Company Institute v. Camp reading so regulators and courts could not narrow the separation by interpretation.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers. The bill separated insured checking and savings deposits from securities trading and underwriting, reducing the chance that bank losses from securities activities force a taxpayer-funded rescue, and reducing conflicts of interest where a bank pushes its own securities on customers. Bank employees and communities also gain from safer banks that fail less often.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits insured depository institutions from being affiliated with brokers, dealers, investment advisers, or investment companies, directly separating insured deposits from securities businesses [S2] [S3].

Repeals the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act provisions (section 4(k)-(o) of the Bank Holding Company Act and financial subsidiaries authority) that created financial holding companies combining banking with insurance, securities, and merchant banking [S3].

Requires existing bank-securities affiliations to wind down within two years, with limited regulator extensions capped at one additional year and required reports to Congress on every exception granted [S2] [S3].
Bars officers, directors, and employees of securities firms from simultaneously serving on insured bank boards, with a narrow regulator-approved exception [S2] [S3].

Ratifies and locks in the Supreme Court's Investment Company Institute v. Camp interpretation, prohibiting federal banking agencies and courts from adopting narrower readings of the separation [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Financial conglomerates and securities firms. Universal banks built under Gramm-Leach-Bliley — firms that combine commercial banking with securities underwriting, dealing, and financial subsidiaries — would have had two years to divest or dissolve those combinations, giving up the scale, cross-selling, and fee revenues of the conglomerate model. Some customers of large banks could lose one-stop convenience, and the forced divestitures could impose adjustment costs on the market during the wind-down period.

drawbacks.text: The two-year mandatory wind-down of bank-securities affiliations [S3] would require divestitures across major firms at the same time, which critics of forced breakups warn could sell assets into depressed markets and disrupt credit in a downturn.

Many economists argue the 2008 crisis spread mainly through unregulated activities Glass-Steagall never covered, such as mortgage brokers and off-balance-sheet vehicles, so re-erecting the wall would not by itself prevent future bailouts; the bill also imposes adjustment costs on banks without addressing those channels.
Reversing Gramm-Leach-Bliley would eliminate some efficiencies and services of universal banks, and banks could pass reduced profitability through to shareholders and, to some degree, depositors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The central benefit — keeping federally insured deposits away from securities trading and underwriting, and reducing taxpayer exposure to losses from that combination — is real and goes directly to the public, which spent hundreds of billions in 2008 without being consulted on a system the bill would unwind. The honest costs are the disruption and lost scale of a two-year forced break-up of financial conglomerates, and the fact that the bill addresses only part of the risk that caused 2008. On balance the protections for depositors and taxpayers are substantial relative to costs that fall chiefly on the affected firms.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee, which sent it to two subcommittees where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2013 — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Marcy Kaptur introduced the bill on April 12, 2011, with Reps. Moran and Jones as original cosponsors [S1] [S3].

It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on the day of introduction, and on May 2, 2011 to the Subcommittees on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit and on Capital Markets and Government Sponsored Enterprises [S5].
The bill accumulated 84 cosponsors — 80 Democrats and 4 Republicans — but no further action was ever taken, and the Congress ended January 3, 2013 with the bill still in committee [S4] [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial conglomerates and securities firms, which kept the Gramm-Leach-Bliley structure of combined banking, trading, and underwriting intact. Anyone counting on a rebuilt Glass-Steagall wall got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore the Glass-Steagall separation and repeal the Gramm-Leach-Bliley provisions.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup on the bill; it was referred to two subcommittees on May 2, 2011 and died there.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided — 80 Democrats and 4 of the chamber's 242 Republicans — and since the bill never reached a floor vote, no roll-call record exists to measure where the chamber stood.

industries.industry: Financial conglomerates (universal banks with securities and insurance arms)
industries.note: The bill would have forced firms built on the Gramm-Leach-Bliley model to divest their securities and financial-subsidiary operations within two years, breaking the combination of insured deposits with trading and underwriting. Their gain from the bill's death is the continued revenue of the conglomerate model whose losses have historically been backstopped by taxpayers.

The bill barred securities firms' executives from sitting on insured bank boards and cut off affiliation with commercial banks, ending a channel of expansion that opened after 1999. Separately, however, the separation protects independent securities firms from competition against banks that could underwrite at deposit-backed scale.

industries.industry: Community banks and independent commercial banks
industries.note: By removing the ability of deposit-taking banks to combine with securities dealers, the bill would reduce competitive pressure toward universal-banking scale and reduce the risk that affiliated securities losses bring down insured banks. It also constrains the Federal Reserve's authority to grant new combined-activity exceptions, requiring reports to Congress for any exception or extension.
